## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.90579.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.90579.3.sa2)

The short-term administration of reprogramming factors to partially reprogram cells has gained traction in recent years as a potential strategy to reverse aging in cells and organisms. Early studies used Yamanaka factors in transgenic mice to reverse aging phenotypes, but chemical cocktails could present a more feasible approach for in vivo delivery. In this study, Mitchell et al sought to determine the effects that short-term administration of chemical reprogramming cocktails have on biological age and function. To address this question, they treated young and old mouse fibroblasts with chemical reprogramming cocktails and performed transcriptome, proteome, metabolome, and DNA methylation profiling pre- and post-treatment. For each of these datasets, they identified changes associated with treatment, showing downregulation of some previously identified molecular signatures of aging in both young and old cells. From these data, the authors conclude that partial chemical reprogramming can rejuvenate both young and old fibroblasts.

The main strength of this study is the comprehensive profiling of cells pre- and post-treatment with the reprogramming cocktails, which will be a valuable resource for better understanding the molecular changes induced by chemical reprogramming. The authors highlighted consistent changes across the different datasets that are thought to be associated with aging phenotypes, showing reduction of age-associated signatures previously identified in various tissues.

results.result: The study used fibroblasts isolated from young (4-month-old) and old (20-month-old) male C57BL/6 mice, with passage number ≤4 to maintain an aged phenotype in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 establish the experimental model. C1 describes the source and age of mice, C2 specifies the passage limitation, and C3 provides literature support for the rationale. These methodological details are clearly stated and appropriately justified.

results.result: Two chemical cocktails were used: 7c (7 compounds) capable of reprogramming somatic cells to pluripotency, and 2c (2 compounds) that does not negatively affect cell proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 define the experimental treatments with appropriate citations. The compositions are explicitly stated and the functional properties are supported by literature (Guan et al., 2022; Hou et al., 2013; Lucas and Paine, 2022).

results.result: 2c treatment dramatically increased alkaline phosphatase (AP) activity in both young and old fibroblasts, indicating increased pluripotency, while 7c had no effect on AP activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 and C29 are supported by AP staining data in Figure 1B. The interpretation of AP activity as a pluripotency marker is appropriately cited (Campbell, 2014). The differential effects of 2c vs 7c are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Partial chemical reprogramming with both 2c and 7c strongly increased mitochondrial membrane potential (TMRM fluorescence) in young and old fibroblasts, with appropriate CCCP control validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 present experimental data from Figure 1C with proper controls (C12). Claims C14-C16 provide relevant context from literature about mitochondrial membrane potential and aging. The measurements are appropriately normalized and controlled.

results.result: 7c treatment dramatically increased proton leak and spare respiratory capacity while having minor effects on basal oxygen consumption, indicating increased activity/abundance of mitochondrial OXPHOS complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 are supported by Seahorse experiments (Figure 1D) with appropriate normalization to cell number. The functional measurements directly support the conclusion about OXPHOS complex activity/abundance.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis showed that 7c treatment caused distinct transcriptional changes compared to 2c and control, and that aged fibroblasts maintained aging signatures in vitro, though treatment effects exceeded age-related changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25 are supported by PCA analysis (Figure 2A), differential expression analysis (Figure 2B), and GSEA (Figure 2—supplement 1A). The correlation analysis (C25, ρ>0.8) demonstrates consistency across age groups. Statistical methods are appropriate.

results.result: 2c and 7c treatments had differential effects on pluripotency markers: both upregulated Bend4, Esrrb, and Klf4, but 2c uniquely upregulated Myc and Sox2 while 7c reduced Nanog and Myc, suggesting 7c operates through a different mechanism than OSKM reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C30 are supported by gene expression data (Figure 2C). The differential expression patterns are clearly shown and the mechanistic interpretation (C30) is reasonable given the distinct pluripotency marker profiles, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: 7c treatment significantly reduced splicing-related protein damage by decreasing retained introns with functional consequences, while age showed marginally significant elevation of splicing damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by splicing damage analysis (Figure 2D) and alternative splicing event analysis (Figure 2—supplement 2B-C). The statistical significance is appropriately reported and the mechanistic interpretation is reasonable.

results.result: Gene expression changes from 2c treatment showed positive association with OSKM reprogramming signatures, while 7c did not; both treatments showed negative associations with aging signatures across multiple tissues and species.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 are supported by GSEA analysis (Figure 2E) using established signatures from Kriukov et al., 2022 and Tyshkovskiy et al., 2023. The differential associations between 2c and 7c with OSKM signatures are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Proteomics analysis revealed that 7c had a more profound effect than 2c on the cellular proteome, with strong correlation (ρ>0.7) between protein and mRNA changes, and all mitochondrial OXPHOS complexes (I-V) were upregulated by both treatments.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38, C44, and C50 are supported by TMT proteomics data (Figures 3A-C, 3E). The correlation analysis is appropriate and the upregulation of all OXPHOS complexes is a key finding consistently observed across treatments and age groups.

results.result: GSEA of proteomics data showed aging signatures included upregulation of inflammation, apoptosis, and p53 signaling with downregulation of energy metabolism and DNA repair, while 2c and 7c treatments produced anti-aging effects including upregulation of OXPHOS, TCA cycle, fatty acid metabolism, and mitochondrial translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are supported by comprehensive GSEA analysis (Figure 3D). The pathway enrichments are statistically significant and the anti-aging effects are well-characterized. The paradoxical upregulation of p53 by treatments (C43) is noted as surprising by the authors.

results.result: Proteomics revealed that splicing proteins were downregulated by age and treatments (more by 7c), RNA methylation proteins were upregulated (more by 7c), chaperones were upregulated only by 7c, and collagen proteins showed opposite effects (down in 7c, up in 2c).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C49 are supported by proteomics data (Figure 3E, Figure 3—supplement 2B). The connection between RNA methylation and splicing (C47) is appropriately cited (Covelo-Molares et al., 2018). The differential effects between treatments are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Partial chemical reprogramming demonstrated the ability to reduce molecular signatures of aging at both protein and mRNA levels.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is a summary conclusion supported by correlation analysis (Figure 4) showing negative associations between treatment effects and aging signatures across multiple omics levels. This integrates findings from multiple prior results.

results.result: Phosphoproteomics revealed that both 2c and 7c treatments increased phosphorylation of mitochondrial proteins and consistently activated Prkaca signaling across all conditions, suggesting a shared mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 and C59 are supported by phosphoproteomics GSEA (Figure 5A, Figure 5—supplement 1A) and kinase enrichment analysis (Figure 5B). Prkaca was the only kinase significantly upregulated across all conditions (FDR<0.05).

results.result: Prkaca knockdown to ~25% of basal levels did not significantly affect 7c-induced increase in mitochondrial membrane potential, suggesting Prkaca signaling is either not necessary or residual levels are sufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are based on knockdown experiments (Figure 5C, Figure 5—supplement 1B). While the knockdown is validated by western blot (C60), the lack of effect on TMRM fluorescence (C61) is difficult to interpret definitively. The conclusion (C62) appropriately acknowledges two possibilities, but incomplete knockdown limits mechanistic conclusions.

results.result: Prkaca appeared to localize more strongly to the nucleus during 7c treatment in old fibroblasts.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by confocal microscopy (Figure 5C). However, this is a qualitative observation and quantification would strengthen the conclusion. The functional significance remains speculative.

results.result: 7c treatment induced a steady increase in apoptosis reaching ~20% by day 6, similar to levels reported for OSK/OSKM reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by Annexin V flow cytometry (Figure 5—supplement 1C) with appropriate citation to Cheung et al., 2012. The time course is well-characterized with n=3 biological replicates.

results.result: Metabolomics identified 203 metabolites, with 109 significantly altered by treatments; 7c had a more pronounced effect than 2c, and appeared to divert cells to a different metabolic state rather than specifically reversing age-related changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by HILIC metabolomics (Figure 6A-C). The data are appropriately normalized to protein content. The interpretation (C69) is reasonable given that only some age-affected metabolites were counteracted by treatment.

results.result: S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) was increased by 7c treatment, which could stem from changes in epigenetic regulation through DNA methyltransferase inhibition, especially given decreased Mat2a protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 is well-supported by citations (Lin et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2008). However, C71 is speculative, connecting metabolomics and proteomics data (Figure 6E) without direct mechanistic validation. The interpretation is plausible but requires further experimental support.

results.result: Several purine degradation metabolites positively associated with aging were reduced by 7c treatment.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is supported by metabolomics data and citation to Panyard et al., 2022. The reduction of aging-associated metabolites is consistent with the overall rejuvenation phenotype.

results.result: Transcriptomic clock analysis showed 7c significantly reduced both chronological and biological age in young and old fibroblasts, while 2c only reduced chronological age; old fibroblasts were transcriptionally older but did not show substantial healthspan-associated changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 are supported by transcriptomic clock analysis (Figure 7A) using validated clocks from the authors' lab. The differential effects between clocks (C76-C77) provide nuanced interpretation about the nature of aging in this system. Statistical significance is appropriately reported.

results.result: Epigenetic clock analysis showed consistent DNAmAge reduction with 7c treatment across multiple clocks, while 2c effects were weaker and variable; old fibroblasts were epigenetically older than young, and iPSCs showed DNAmAge ~0, confirming 7c can rejuvenate both young and aged cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are supported by DNA methylation array data (Figure 7B) using multiple established epigenetic clocks. The iPSC control (C81) validates the approach. The consistency across clocks for 7c strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: 7c treatment induced global hypomethylation enriched in transcription/exon regions and depleted in heterochromatin/promoters, pushing cells to a distinct epigenetic landscape independent of initial state.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by DNA methylation analysis (Figure 7—supplement 3C-D) with chromatin state enrichment analysis. The global nature of the effect and its independence from initial state are well-demonstrated.

results.result: Based on multi-omics analyses, partial chemical reprogramming with 7c rejuvenates fibroblasts through upregulation of mitochondrial OXPHOS (the most prominent signature), accompanied by increased apoptosis and reversal of molecular damage including aging-related metabolites and mis-spliced mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 represent the main conclusions integrating multiple lines of evidence from transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, aging clocks, and functional assays. The OXPHOS upregulation is consistently observed across multiple omics levels and is functionally validated by Seahorse experiments.

results.result: The authors propose that partial chemical reprogramming induces rejuvenation at least in part by upregulating mitochondrial OXPHOS, which is known to decline with aging and whose augmentation can increase longevity.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 integrate the study's findings with established literature (Tyshkovskiy et al., 2019, 2023; Berry et al., 2023a,b). The mechanistic proposal (C93) is reasonable given the consistent OXPHOS upregulation and its known relationship to aging, though causality is not directly demonstrated.

results.result: The effects of partial chemical reprogramming were similar in young and old fibroblasts, possibly because treatment effects exceeded age-related changes or because treatments push cells to a different metabolic state that makes them biologically younger as a byproduct.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 provide important context and interpretation. C94 is supported by citation (Nishimura et al., 2019). C95 is an observation from the data. C96-C97 are speculative interpretations that are reasonable given the data but not directly tested.

results.result: The study concludes that partial chemical reprogramming can reverse many signs of aging and may represent a viable alternative to OSKM reprogramming, potentially circumventing limitations including low efficiency, oncogenic risk, and toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C98 and C101 are supported by the study's data. However, C99 and C102 are speculative about potential advantages over OSKM reprogramming. C100 appropriately cites limitations of OSKM approaches, but direct comparisons and in vivo validation are needed to support claims of superiority.

results.result: The authors acknowledge important limitations: the study used only one cell type from inbred male mice, and note that different cell types age differently and interventions show sex-dimorphic effects, requiring extensive validation in diverse systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C106 appropriately acknowledge study limitations with supporting citations (Kimmel et al., 2019; Sampathkumar et al., 2020). This demonstrates scientific rigor in recognizing the scope and generalizability of the findings.

results.result: The study used fibroblasts from young (4-month) and old (20-month) male mice with limited passage numbers (≤4) to preserve aged phenotype. Gene expression analysis confirmed that 20-month-old fibroblasts showed positive associations with aging signatures and negative associations with iPSC signatures, demonstrating that the aged phenotype was preserved in vitro at the transcriptional level.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed the study design and validation of the aged phenotype. One reviewer stated the authors 'provide solid evidence to support their claim' and another noted the 'multi-omics data was collected' with appropriate analyses. No concerns were raised about the experimental model or age validation.

results.result: 2c treatment dramatically increased alkaline phosphatase (AP) activity in both young and old fibroblasts and upregulated pluripotency markers (Myc, Sox2, Esrrb, Klf4, Bend4), showing a more pronounced pro-pluripotency effect similar to OSKM reprogramming. In contrast, 7c treatment had no effect on AP activity and paradoxically reduced Nanog and Myc expression, suggesting a different mechanism than normal OSKM cellular reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. The comprehensive profiling was noted as a 'main strength' and the data showing 'downregulation of some previously identified molecular signatures of aging' was acknowledged. The differential effects of 2c versus 7c were implicitly accepted through the reviewers' positive assessment of the multi-omics approach.

results.result: Partial chemical reprogramming, particularly with 7c, strongly increased mitochondrial membrane potential (TMRM fluorescence) and upregulated mitochondrial OXPHOS complexes (I-V) in both young and old fibroblasts. 7c treatment dramatically increased proton leak and spare respiratory capacity, while having only minor effects on basal oxygen consumption. This upregulation of mitochondrial OXPHOS was identified as the most prominent mechanistic signature of partial chemical reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly supported these findings, with one stating the authors 'provide solid evidence' for changes consistent with biological age reduction. Another reviewer noted the study 'highlighted consistent changes across the different datasets that are thought to be associated with aging phenotypes.' The mitochondrial findings were central to the reviewers' positive assessment.

results.result: 7c treatment significantly lowered splicing-related protein damage by decreasing retained introns with functional consequences, while proteins for mRNA splicing were downregulated and RNA methylation proteins were upregulated. This represents reversal of molecular damage associated with aging, including mis-spliced mRNA accumulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as part of the comprehensive multi-omics analysis. One reviewer noted the study showed 'downregulation of some previously identified molecular signatures of aging,' which would include splicing damage. No concerns were raised about the splicing analysis or interpretation.

results.result: Gene expression changes induced by both 2c and 7c were negatively associated with aging signatures across different tissues and species. Treatment produced anti-aging effects including upregulation of OXPHOS, TCA cycle, fatty acid metabolism, and mitochondrial translation, and downregulation of interferon signaling. Aging signatures showed upregulation of inflammation, apoptosis, and p53 signaling, with downregulation of energy metabolism and DNA repair.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings. One stated the authors 'provide solid evidence to support their claim that chemical reprogramming factors induce changes consistent with a reduction of cellular biological age (e.g., correlations with established aging markers in whole tissues).' The comprehensive nature of the anti-aging effects was noted as a strength.

results.result: Both 2c and 7c treatments upregulated phosphorylation of mitochondrial proteins, with Prkaca signaling being the only kinase pathway significantly and consistently upregulated across all treatments and age groups. However, Prkaca knockdown experiments showed that TMRM fluorescence was not affected, suggesting Prkaca signaling is either not necessary for the mitochondrial membrane potential increase or residual Prkaca is sufficient. Prkaca appeared to localize more strongly to the nucleus during 7c treatment in old fibroblasts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the phosphoproteomics findings as part of the comprehensive multi-omics dataset. One reviewer noted 'different analyses were conducted accordingly, including differential expression analysis, gene set enrichment analysis' and that 'the impact of partial chemical reprogramming on aging was supported by these multi-source results.' The Prkaca findings were not specifically challenged.

results.result: During 7c treatment, there was a steady increase in apoptotic cells reaching approximately 20% by day 6, similar to OSK/OSKM reprogramming. This increase in apoptosis accompanied the increase in OXPHOS activity, suggesting partial chemical reprogramming might remove cells with dysfunctional mitochondria.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the apoptosis findings. The comprehensive profiling approach was praised, and the apoptosis data fit within the accepted narrative of the study's findings. One reviewer noted the study as 'important' and providing 'solid evidence,' implicitly accepting all major findings including apoptosis.

results.result: Metabolomics analysis identified 203 metabolites, with 109 significantly altered by partial chemical reprogramming. 7c treatment had a much more pronounced effect on the metabolome than 2c, appearing to divert cells to a different metabolic state rather than targeting specific aging-related changes. Changes included increased S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), which could stem from epigenetic regulation changes, and decreased purine degradation metabolites associated with aging.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the metabolomics findings as part of the comprehensive multi-omics approach. One reviewer specifically noted 'multi-omics data was collected, including epigenome, transcriptome, proteome, phosphoproteome, and metabolome' and that these analyses supported the impact on aging. No concerns were raised about the metabolomics interpretation.

results.result: Application of transcriptomic and epigenetic clocks revealed that 7c treatment significantly decreased both predicted chronological and biological age in young and old fibroblasts, with consistent lowering of DNA methylation age. 2c treatment showed weaker and more variable effects. Old fibroblasts were epigenetically older than young fibroblasts, confirming aged phenotype preservation. Fully-reprogrammed iPSCs showed epigenetic age of approximately 0. The authors concluded that partial chemical reprogramming, particularly with 7c, can rejuvenate both young and aged cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly supported these findings. One stated the authors 'provide solid evidence to support their claim that chemical reprogramming factors induce changes consistent with a reduction of cellular biological age.' Another noted 'transcriptomic and epigenetic clock-based analyses' were among the strengths, and 'the impact of partial chemical reprogramming on aging was supported by these multi-source results.'

results.result: 7c treatment induced global hypomethylation rather than targeting specific age-related CpG sites. Hypomethylated sites were enriched in transcription and exon regions and depleted in heterochromatin and promoter regions. This signature was shared in both young and old fibroblasts, suggesting 7c pushes cells to a distinct epigenetic landscape independent of their initial state.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the epigenetic findings as part of the comprehensive analysis. The epigenetic clock results were specifically mentioned as a strength, and the global hypomethylation mechanism was not challenged. One reviewer noted the study provides 'solid evidence' for biological age reduction, which encompasses these epigenetic changes.

results.result: Partial chemical reprogramming causes wide-scale changes to gene expression larger in magnitude than aging-related changes, with similar effects in both young and old fibroblasts across most assays. The authors propose that 7c pushes cells to a different metabolic state that makes them biologically younger as a byproduct, potentially by activating a unique set of transcription factors producing an epigenetically-distinct cellular state.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these interpretations without challenge. One noted the 'comprehensive profiling of cells pre- and post-treatment' as a main strength, and another stated the findings were 'supported by these multi-source results.' The mechanistic interpretations were implicitly accepted through the reviewers' overall positive assessment.

results.result: The authors conclude that partial chemical reprogramming induces rejuvenation at least in part by upregulating mitochondrial OXPHOS, which differs from OSKM reprogramming's glycolytic shift. They propose that partial chemical reprogramming with 7c features a distinct mechanism from OSK/OSKM and may represent a viable alternative for rejuvenating aged cells, potentially circumventing risks of OSK/OSKM reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Reviewers supported these conclusions. One stated the study is 'important' and provides 'solid evidence,' while another noted it will be 'a valuable resource for better understanding the molecular changes induced by chemical reprogramming.' The distinct mechanism from OSKM was implicitly accepted through the reviewers' positive assessment of the comprehensive findings.

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations including that the study used only one cell type from inbred male mice, and note that further testing in animal models is needed to elucidate in vivo effectiveness. They cite that different cell types experience varying aging changes and that aging effects are generally sex-dimorphic.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these acknowledged limitations. The study was described as 'important' and providing 'solid evidence' despite these limitations. The reviewers' acceptance of the study's conclusions implicitly acknowledges that these limitations do not undermine the core findings within the stated scope.
